title: What time is the 2026 Bahrain GP and how can I watch it?
excerpt:
Formula 1 moves on to Sepang this weekend for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia – and here are the global start times for Sunday’s race.

George Russell put in a dominant performance last weekend in Azerbaijan to claim victory and close the gap to Mercedes team mate Kimi Antonelli in the drivers' standings to 66 points. Will Mercedes win again, or can Max Verstappen finally claim his first win of the 2026 season after just missing out in Baku?

Head to the RACE HUB or scroll down for more on how and when you can watch the action, along with the global start times for each session.

What time is the 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia?

Free Practice 1 will kick off the weekend on Friday, October 2 at 1230 local time, with Free Practice 2 following at 1600.

Free Practice 3 takes place at 1230 on Saturday, October 3, ahead of Qualifying at 1600 before the Grand Prix itself gets underway at 1500 on Sunday, October 4.

Check out the image below to find all the global start times for Sunday’s race.

How can I watch the 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia?

You can enjoy coverage from every session live on F1 TV Pro (available in selected countries), which brings fans closer to the action via exclusive features like onboard cameras on all 22 of the drivers’ cars, and access to both Pre-Race and Post-Race Shows.

F1 TV Pro can be streamed easily via Apple TV, Chromecast Generation 2 and above, Android TV, Google TV, Amazon Fire TV, and Roku. F1 TV Pro is free of ad breaks and available with commentary in six languages.

Fans can also watch via F1 TV Premium, a premier service that invites fans to step into the heart of the action with the ability to watch races in 4K Ultra HD/HDR on up to six different devices, as well as a personalised Multiview feature available on select devices with 26 different feeds to choose from.

Viewers can watch every F1 Grand Prix, F1 Sprint, Qualifying and practice session live in 4K Ultra HD/HDR at home, with F2, F3, F1 ACADEMY and Porsche Supercup sessions also available to watch live on the platform.

Alternatively, live timing will be available on F1.com and the F1 app across every session during the Grand Prix weekend.

Where is the 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia taking place?

The Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia will be held at the Sepang International Circuit, the venue having last hosted an F1 race in 2017 after being introduced to the calendar in 1999.

With this year's earlier Bahrain Grand Prix postponed, a new date and venue will now welcome the event for the 16th round of the season.

The circuit is known for its mixture of fast, flowing sections combined with long straights, while high humidity and intense heat will test the drivers' fitness.

Verstappen was the driver to win when F1 last visited the Malaysian venue, while both Lewis Hamilton and Fernando Alonso have also stood on the top step previously.

What is the weather forecast in Sepang?

As things stand, the weather looks set to be warm and humid for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia weekend, with sunny spells, light winds and a chance of a rain shower.

The region is known for its high humidity and thunderstorms that threaten to develop and cause a deluge at short notice.

title: Why a return to Sepang is a 'golden ticket' for F1 drivers
excerpt:
Formula 1 drivers are eagerly awaiting this weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia and the sport’s return to Sepang after a nine-year absence.

The circuit hosted the Malaysian Grand Prix 19 times between 1999 and the most recent event in 2017. The first of a new generation of permanent venues – followed by the likes of Bahrain, Shanghai, Istanbul and Abu Dhabi among others – at the time, the track set new standards in terms of facilities.

It always produced good racing, with drivers enjoying its flowing layout and overtaking opportunities. Weather always played a part, with the hot and humid conditions making it a tough challenge for the drivers, while rain was always a possibility.

And that adds an extra dimension to this event given that we have made it to Round 16 and still not seen a fully wet session in 2026, never mind a race.

Despite the track’s long absence from the calendar, 10 of the drivers on the current grid have raced at Sepang, namely Fernando Alonso (first start in 2001), Lewis Hamilton (2007), Nico Hulkenberg (2010), Sergio Perez (2011), Valtteri Bottas (2013), Carlos Sainz (2015), Max Verstappen (2015), Esteban Ocon (2016), Pierre Gasly (2017) and Lance Stroll (2017).

None of them know Sepang as well as Alonso, who won in 2005 with Renault, in 2007 with McLaren, and in 2012 with Ferrari. Given his good record there, it’s perhaps not surprising that the Aston Martin driver is keen to return.

“Yeah, I’m looking forward,” he said. “I didn't think that I will race in Malaysia again, so that's a golden ticket that I take. An incredible circuit, demanding race, temperature, humidity – like Singapore, but in daytime.

“So it will be also a good test for drivers, and yeah, looking forward. I think from the remaining races, probably Sepang is the nicest track. So let's see.”

Hamilton finished second to Alonso in what was his second ever F1 start in 2007, and he went on to win the race in 2014.

He has also spent more time in Kuala Lumpur than his fellow drivers thanks to his long relationship with Mercedes title sponsor Petronas.

“I always loved going to KL had lots of great experiences there with my previous team,” he said. “And the track is awesome. And it's a track that does give good racing.

“So I very much welcome it, I'm looking forward to it. It's a super-hot circuit. It’s going to be one that's physically massively demanding, so I look forward to that challenge.”

10 quiz questions on F1 at the Sepang International Circuit

Hamilton stressed that the physical side is an important part of being an F1 driver.

“This is supposed to be the sport that's the most physically demanding, mentally and physically,” he said. “And there are some that are just so hot, and ultimately you are on the edge. Like Singapore is incredibly hot and demanding.

“Malaysia will be crazy this year, but that's where I think you want to see athletes just right at the edge of their performance, having to actually push their bodies further. Because that's what this sport is about – pushing the levels, and pushing the boundaries.”

The other past Sepang winner in the current field is Verstappen, who triumphed in 2017. So is the Red Bull driver looking forward to going back?

“Actually not, because I was actually quite happy that I won the final one there!” he joked. “No, I think it's a great track. I really enjoy being there. It's very tough I think just from the heat already, but also degradation will be really tough on the tyres. So yeah, it's a nice place. So excited to go back and see we can do there.”

So what of the 12 drivers who have yet to race at Sepang? They’ve all been busy in factory simulators, but one of them has a little more experience than the others.

"Malaysia, I'm excited for,” said Lando Norris. “It's one I've seen many races on when I was younger, and growing up. And actually, I remember I did sim support for Fernando and Stoffel [Vandoorne] when they raced there many years ago.

“So I remember going into the factory at midnight or whatever stupid time it was, and driving till 7am just to support the guys. So it's not completely new to me, but it'll be a first time going to the circuit itself, which is exciting.”

For everyone else, Sepang is a track that they know only from watching past races on TV and their recent simulator runs.

“I think it's always very nice as a driver to discover a new track,” said World Championship leader Kimi Antonelli. “I've done it on the sim, and it looks like a pretty cool track.

"Very fast, flowing, long corners, not easy, especially to put the lap together. I think it's going to be very interesting as well with tyre degradation. We might see two, three stops, because tyre deg is going to be big.

“But another question mark is going to be the weather. I've seen the forecast, and it seems to rain pretty heavily at a specific time of the day. So there's going to be a lot of unknowns. Obviously, it's going to be very, very hot. It's going to be a good challenge – and I’m looking forward to it.”

title: 5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the Bahrain GP
excerpt:
Fresh from a thrilling finish in Baku it’s time to return to another popular venue for the first time in nearly a decade. George Russell heads to the relocated Bahrain Grand Prix in fine form, but it will be a new test for many of the drivers as we look ahead to the next round of the triple-header in Sepang.

Can Russell build momentum?

The Azerbaijan Grand Prix was a very impressive weekend for Russell, as he secured his third win of the season. What was notable was how comfortable he looked right from the opening lap, topping the first practice sessions, taking a dominant pole position and then leading every lap on his way to victory.

That doesn’t tell the full story either, as Russell had to withstand serious pressure from Max Verstappen in the second half of the race, but did not crack as he picked up his first Grand Prix win since Austria in late June.

With Kimi Antonelli having a tough opening two days in Azerbaijan before recovering from 16th on the grid to fifth, Russell closed the gap at the top of the Drivers’ Championship from 81 points to 66. That’s still a significant margin, and Antonelli has been remarkably consistent this year, but Russell has certainly looked more comfortable himself since the summer break.

The races come quickly at this stage of the season and – as long as he doesn’t take a power unit penalty – if Russell can carry over his form from Baku to Sepang, then he’ll have every chance of reducing Antonelli’s advantage once again.

Mercedes have an upgrade

This could well be an ominous entry for Mercedes’ rivals, given the fact the Constructors’ Championship leaders have won the past three races, but there will be new parts on the W17 this weekend.

Mercedes had suggested they would face a tough test in August and September as rivals were updating their cars, and there was a run of one win in four races prior to the latest three victories. But what was already a very competitive car is set for a further upgrade.

Three practice sessions should give Mercedes time to understand the impact of their package, and it will be up to the drivers to get their heads round any potential changes in the car characteristics. However, despite an impressive rate of improvement across the grid so far this season, the success of an update is never guaranteed.

Esteban Ocon on the market

Only a week ago we featured the driver market going through a quiet spell, but in Azerbaijan there was some movement as Esteban Ocon described himself as a free agent for 2027.

Haas Team Principal Ayao Komatsu clarified that had technically been the case since the summer – when the window opened for an option on Ocon’s contract being taken up – but the Frenchman very much gave the impression that he would not be remaining with the team next year.

Who are the favourites for the Haas seats in 2027?

Ocon pointed to his performance in Baku – where he finished eighth ahead of team mate Ollie Bearman in ninth – as proof that he deserves his place on the grid. But options for another race seat are limited at this stage, especially now that Aston Martin have confirmed an unchanged line-up, so it remains to be seen where he might land.

At the same time, if Ocon is indeed a free agent then attention will also turn to who will replace him at Haas, where both seats are currently unconfirmed. Rafael Camara did his chances no harm by taking the lead of the Formula 2 Championship in Baku with a Feature Race victory, but reserve driver Jack Doohan recently completed a test outing for Haas, as have Ryo Hirakawa and Leonardo Fornaroli.

Internal team dynamics

It was a dramatic second half of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, and the first Safety Car restart saw all sorts of chaos that also involved two sets of team mates.

Misjudgements from Franco Colapinto and Arvid Lindblad saw them hit and spin their team mates Pierre Gasly and Liam Lawson respectively, taking both out of the running for points. Lando Norris was also caught up in the incident that saw Gasly and Colapinto retire, while Lawson suffered damage, but Lindblad could at least limit the losses by recovering to finish seventh.

Alpine consider 'what action should be taken' after Colapinto crash

Colapinto has a five-place grid penalty for this weekend’s race in Malaysia as a result of causing a collision, and Alpine Executive Advisor Flavio Briatore suggested there could be further internal repercussions.

“I know that Franco has taken full responsibility for it, as he should; in fact he braked far too late considering the context of the race and the Safety Car restart,” Briatore said after Baku. “It was a very poor move for a driver of his experience. I want to take time to reflect on it and consider what course of action should be taken, so we can learn from it and avoid such a situation in future.”

This weekend will likely see the fallout discussed further, but it also provides all of the drivers involved with a chance to bounce back quickly. If it impacts the dynamics between team mates – particularly if they are racing wheel-to-wheel again at any stage on Sunday – remains to be seen.

A fond return to Sepang

Following the postponement of the Bahrain Grand Prix in April, strong collaboration between the Sakhir race organisers and the Government of Malaysia led to the agreement to host this year’s edition of the race in Sepang.

The circuit was last on the calendar in 2017, having hosted the Malaysian Grand Prix on 19 occasions. During that time, it delivered plenty of exciting racing, with the long straights that start and end the lap providing overtaking opportunities, while the high-speed middle sector is also a great test of all-round car performance.

Throw in the potential for rain to impact the action and all of the ingredients are in place for an exciting return this weekend. Ten drivers have previously made a Grand Prix start at Sepang, meaning more than half of the grid will be getting their first taste of racing action at the venue.

While it is a shame not to be able to race in Bahrain – on a track that often delivers plenty of close battles – there’s every chance that Sepang can offer a similarly entertaining Grand Prix as a substitute over the coming days.

title: Where does Russell’s Baku win rank in the closest F1 finishes?
excerpt:
Max Verstappen chased George Russell all the way to the line at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, coming just 0.196s shy of snatching the win away from the Mercedes driver.

It was a gap more than four times smaller than Russell’s pole position advantage, and among the closest winning margins in the history of Formula 1 – but it falls 0.014s and one position shy of squeaking into the top 10 closest F1 finishes ever.

So which races have been won by even less than that? Our in-house data team have got the top 10...

10. 2002 Austrian Grand Prix – 0.182s

Ferrari dominated the 2002 season but at the sixth round of the year invoked team orders that were among the most controversial in history.

Rubens Barrichello headed Michael Schumacher, and for a second successive year was instructed to allow the team leader through. But whereas in 2001 it was for second place, in 2002 it was for the win.

Barrichello did so exiting the final corner, and a hesitant Schumacher also slowed in response, the pair crawling over the line split by 0.182s in Schumacher’s favour. A farcical podium ceremony took place, with Schumacher insisting Barrichello stand on the top step, with the Brazilian being handed the winner’s trophy. Fines followed.

PALMER: Why Russell’s Baku win was so impressive

9. 2023 Australian Grand Prix – 0.179s

Australia’s race in 2023 was a messy encounter, amid a record number of red flags, and several standing starts.

The last of those triggered more carnage, and proceedings were suspended once more; with no more racing laps remaining when the signal was given for the rolling restart drivers were greeted with the chequered flag.

Long-time race leader Max Verstappen thus crossed the line, followed by Lewis Hamilton, with no overtaking permitted. The gap between the pair was a notional 0.179s but it was not remotely indicative of a closely-fought Grand Prix, as Verstappen was 10 seconds up the road until the late melees.

8. 2000 Canadian Grand Prix – 0.174s

A second appearance already on this list for Michael Schumacher and Rubens Barrichello (and, spoiler alert: it won’t be their last).

Schumacher led Barrichello in a dry/wet race in Canada, but during the closing stages in increasingly treacherous conditions his Ferrari developed a brake problem, and having retired from the previous round in Monaco reaching the flag was a priority.

With breathing room to the remainder of the field, Schumacher was able to back off slightly across the last laps – going almost four seconds slower on the last lap – to nurse the car to the finish.

Barrichello, who was then still chasing his maiden win, dutifully followed him home in second.

7. 1961 French Grand Prix – 0.1s

In the early 1960s timing data only went down to one decimal place, so that was what split Giancarlo Baghetti and Dan Gurney after 52 laps of racing around Reims’ high-speed roads, the course having only five corners of note.

Other challengers fell by the wayside, and so Baghetti and Gurney duelled, with the former out-dragging the latter to the finish line.

Baghetti also became the only driver aside from Nino Farina, who won the inaugural Grand Prix (excluding the anomalous Indianapolis 500 when it was part of the championship), to take a debut win.

6. 1954 French Grand Prix – 0.1s

Mercedes’ first foray into Formula 1 lasted only 12 Grands Prix in the 1950s but it was a supremely successful spell all the same, as they won nine of them.

The first of those wins came on their debut at Reims, entering the championship mid-season once the W196 was finally ready for action.

The streamlined bodywork was fitted to the new car for Reims’ high-speed straights, and Mercedes dominated. Team orders were imposed, and the great Juan Manuel Fangio led Karl Kling for a 1-2. They were the only drivers to finish the race on the lead lap.

5. 1969 Italian Grand Prix – 0.08s

The first of two appearances for Monza on the list, which is perhaps unsurprising given the high-speed track is renowned for its slipstream battles.

The 1969 encounter was an all-time classic, as four drivers battled for the lead, and Jean-Pierre Beltoise grabbed the inside line into Parabolica on the last of the 68 laps.

But Jackie Stewart got the cutback and overhauled Beltoise, while Jochen Rindt shadowed Stewart and finished just 0.08s behind the Matra.

Beltoise had to make do with third, and Bruce McLaren ensured the top four flashed past the spectators separated by just 0.019s.

4. 1982 Austrian Grand Prix – 0.05s

Alain Prost held an advantage of almost half a minute at the Osterreichring but with five of the 52 laps left to run his Renault met a fiery and smoky demise.

That left Elio de Angelis and Keke Rosberg up front, as both pursued their first wins. De Angelis’ advantage as they began the final lap was a comfortable 1.6 seconds, but Rosberg put in a monster last lap to close in as they raced around the hills.

De Angelis hugged the inside line through the final two right-hand sweeps but Rosberg’s greater speed enabled him to draw alongside as they hurtled along the start/finish straight. De Angelis ultimately held on, but only by half a car’s length.

POWER RANKINGS: Who impressed our judges in Baku?

3. 1986 Spanish Grand Prix – 0.014s

Spain returned to the Formula 1 calendar after a five-year absence and it was a first appearance at Jerez.

Alain Prost, Nigel Mansell and Ayrton Senna battled for honours and put on a classic, with Senna moving into the lead after Mansell pitted for fresh tyres.

Across the final laps Mansell surged up to the rear of Senna’s Lotus but the Brazilian naturally made his car as wide as possible. Mansell got a great exit from the final hairpin on the last lap and ducked out from behind the slipstream, but Senna managed to hold on by a margin of just 0.014s.

2. 2002 United States Grand Prix – 0.011s

By the time Formula 1 arrived at the Brickyard in 2002, Michael Schumacher had long since wrapped up his fifth Drivers’ title and Ferrari another Constructors’ crown, and unsurprisingly the F2002s were again the class of the field.

Schumacher controlled the race, but slowed on the last lap to stage a side-by-side finish, and after brief uncertainty – while the drivers pointed to each other and tried to figure it out – it was judged that Rubens Barrichello had nosed ahead by 0.011s.

There was speculation that it was payback for the saga in Austria earlier in the year, though Schumacher only went as far as claiming he was trying to engineer a dead heat.

1. 1971 Italian Grand Prix – 0.01s

Monza’s 1971 race was the last before two chicanes were introduced to the track in a bid to reduce speeds slightly, and its old layout certainly signed off with a humdinger.

A few of the pre-race favourites retired in the early stages, and subsequently the race developed into a slipstream battle involving several drivers.

Five cars ran line astern across the final lap, scrapping fiercely as they raced to Parabolica, and it was Peter Gethin who emerged in front.

Ronnie Peterson challenged Gethin to the line and they crossed side-by-side, but by a hair’s breadth it was Gethin who triumphed. Francois Cevert was third at 0.09s, Mike Hailwood fourth at 0.18s, and Howard Ganley a comparatively whopping 0.61s behind in fifth.

title: The encouraging signs hidden within McLaren's Baku upgrade
excerpt:
McLaren turned up at Baku with a big upgrade but although its introduction did not go as smoothly as the team’s previous packages – there were some repairs necessary after the first day of practice – the team was satisfied that the changes brought the improvements they sought.

From the outside, it was difficult to judge how big an improvement because the nature of the Baku track was fundamentally unsuited to the McLaren, with the long Caspian ‘straight’ punishing the car’s short gearing and the slow, short corners not playing to the car’s strength in long, fast turns.

title: F1 Business Summit adds new Las Vegas speakers
excerpt:
Haas Team Principal Ayao Komatsu will sit for an on-stage Q&A at the F1 Business Summit in Las Vegas, as part of a programme that also brings in chef Gordon Ramsay, Super Bowl-winning quarterback Russell Wilson and three-time Olympic snowboarding champion Shaun White.

The Summit takes place on Thursday 19 November 2026 at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace, two days before the Las Vegas Grand Prix. It is a ticketed event, hosted by actress, comedian and podcast host Heather McMahan.

Who is speaking?

Komatsu's session covers what it takes to run an F1 team against far larger rivals, taking in leadership, innovation and resilience.

Wilson, White and fellow Super Bowl winner Ndamukong Suh make up the keynote panel, which looks at how athletes turn a competitive career into ownership and investment once the playing days are over. Ramsay's session examines his partnership with F1 and the business of feeding a race weekend, while Jean Arnault appears in a featured spotlight on the sport's partnership with LVMH.

A panel on the modern fan brings together Cadillac Chief Marketing Officer Ahmed "Meddy" Iqbal, CAA Sports International President Matthew O'Donohoe and WHOOP Chief Marketing Officer Dirk-Jan van Hameren, with former Eurosport Chief Executive Peter Hutton moderating. Further sessions cover fashion, hospitality and how circuits around the world promote their races, with Silverstone Chief Executive Stuart Pringle OBE among those taking part.

F1 President and Chief Executive Officer Stefano Domenicali will give opening remarks alongside Steve Hill of the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority, with Liberty Media President and Chief Executive Derek Chang closing proceedings.

"The F1 Business Summit rounds out an incredible week of events in Las Vegas, bringing together an impressive lineup of industry leaders for conversations that extend well beyond the track," said Domenicali.

"This year’s programming will explore the evolving role sports play in shaping brand relevance, storytelling and cultural connection. Las Vegas provides the perfect backdrop for these discussions, and we’re excited to create a forum that brings together new perspectives and adds to the energy that makes race week unlike anything else."

Why the Las Vegas Grand Prix is special

What else is new?

SPORT BEACH joins as presenting partner of the keynote panel and will bring its Clubhouse experience trackside on the Thursday evening for VIP package holders.

The Summit itself runs from 8am to 1pm, opening with an hour-long networking breakfast. Tickets start at $550, with a VIP package at $2,500, and are available at f1lasvegasgp.com.

And the racing?

The 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix runs from 19–21 November, with the race itself on the Saturday night – 50 laps of the 6.2km (3.8 miles) Las Vegas Strip Circuit, where cars pass the casinos at more than 346kph (215kph). With average speeds similar to Monza, otherwise known as F1’s ‘Temple of Speed’, there'll be plenty of action.

title: Why Alonso has re-signed with Aston Martin
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso's love affair with Formula 1 will continue as the Spaniard has opted to stick around for at least another year with Aston Martin.

The double World Champion will turn 46 next year, which still leaves him nine years shy of F1's oldest driver to start a race, Louis Chiron, but comfortably the oldest of the recent generation.

Alonso took his time to make his decision because he knew Aston Martin would wait for him while he pondered his future and whether he fancied another season with a project that has really struggled this year.

The British team are 10th in the Teams' Championship and required a B-spec update in Hungary to haul them into the midfield – having previously been more than five seconds off the pace at times.

Even with that step forward, their engine supplier Honda – who Alonso had a difficult relationship with when they struggled with McLaren – are well off in terms of performance while reliability has been less than ideal.

Though Aston Martin hope next year will be better, no one can be certain that it will be and thus Alonso risks not being able to fight for positions much further up the field.

However, after having conversations with boss Lawrence Stroll and Team Principal Adrian Newey – alongside plenty of private thought to mull what he wants from life going forward – Alonso decided to stay.

The Spaniard loves Formula 1 and can't imagine a life without being behind the wheel of one of the sport's cars in the near future, even if it might mean battling in the midfield rather than for podiums and wins.

He still believes he's fast and it's clear he is still motivated to be in the best physical and mental shape possible to deliver on his immense talent.

Aston Martin keep Alonso and Stroll for 2027

His drive to ninth in the Dutch Grand Prix was proof he's still got the hunger, fight, determination and speed. Now it's just down to Aston Martin to give him a car to make the most of that skillset.

Alonso clearly believes they can and he has full faith in Newey – the greatest technical mind the sport has ever seen – to turn things around but he also accepts that much of whether that becomes reality is out of his hands.

The best he can do is stay, throw his full support behind the team and do everything in his power to get the best out of the package every time he drives so they know exactly what the package is capable of.

And it'll mean another year where his son Leonard, who was born earlier this year, will get the chance to watch his father do what he loves to do – something which is important to Alonso.

For Aston Martin, keeping him in the race seat is a big win. Alonso was always likely to stay in some role, as he's committed to the project for the long term, but they know what he's still capable of when he's driving.

It shows belief in the project, which will then trickle down through the team and help serve as motivation.

Alongside him will be Lance Stroll, whom Alonso has raced alongside since 2023.

Stroll has had the raw end of the unreliability this year – he's retired 11 times in 2026 – but his father believes he has what it takes to win races and fight for championships.

The Canadian believes in the project and says he's committed to helping the team achieve their goals. At over 200 Grands Prix, he has plenty of experience to help with that cause.

The 2027 grid is nearer completion

There are just four seats remaining on the 2027 grid.

Two of those are at Haas with Ollie Bearman favourite to stay with the team for a third full season as he continues to go from strength to strength.

His team mate is set to change, though, with Esteban Ocon a free agent and understood to have accepted he won't be staying on with the American squad in 2027.

Who are the favourites for the Haas seats in 2027?

Ferrari junior and FIA Formula 2 Championship leader Rafael Camara is favourite to get the nod, having had competition from McLaren reserve driver Leo Fornaroli and Haas reserves Jack Doohan and Ryo Hirakawa.

That leaves two seats at Racing Bulls. One is set to go to rookie Arvid Lindblad, who is on a run of nine points finishes in 10 Grands Prix.

Liam Lawson is the frontrunner to partner him for another year, having impressed both with Racing Bulls and during his three-race super-sub stint with Red Bull for the injured Isack Hadjar.

However, there remains a chance Red Bull and Racing Bulls opt to promote rising star Nikola Tsolov, who is currently second in the F2 championship, just seven points shy of Camara.

title: Aston Martin keep Alonso and Stroll for 2027
excerpt:
Aston Martin will race an unchanged line-up in 2027 with Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll extending their long-term contracts with the British team.

While Stroll had been expected to stay on for a ninth season, Alonso's future was less certain given the team's poor performance so far this year.

Alonso said: “I'm very happy to sign a new contract with Aston Martin. I took my time to make this decision, but racing is my life, my passion, and I know I still have the speed and determination to compete at the highest level.

“I’m committed for the long term with this team and to helping us succeed. I truly believe in what we are building: we have strong leadership, incredible people, partners and facilities.

“I look forward to making more memories on the race track in front of the passionate fans. Their energy creates an atmosphere that inspires me and is what makes our sport special.”

How Carlos Alcaraz's bromance with Alonso made him an F1 fan

Stroll added: “I’m very happy to continue with Aston Martin Aramco for the long term. I’ve been on this journey since the beginning and I believe we have the resources and the people to become a winning team.

“There is so much hard work going on at Silverstone with real progress being made, and the determination I see in every department is a huge motivation for me.

“I know we are heading in the right direction, and my commitment is stronger than ever to help us achieve our goals.”

Executive Chairman Lawrence Stroll said: “Lance and Fernando have been a crucial part of our journey and we are very pleased to confirm that they will continue with us into the next chapter for the team.

“Having two drivers with their level of experience, commitment and knowledge provides tremendous value to the whole organisation.

“We are here to win, and whilst our short-term focus remains on improving performance, I believe we have the world-class talent we need to achieve our long-term objectives.”

That leaves just four seats free on the 2027 grid.

Haas are expected to announce Ollie Bearman will stay on, with FIA Formula 2 Championship leader Rafael Camara the frontrunner to be his team mate.

Racing Bulls are expected to retain Arvid Lindblad for a second year. Liam Lawson is hoping to get another full season but there remains a chance they will promote Nikola Tsolov, who is currently second in F2.

title: Aston Martin reduce financial loss as huge F1 expansion complete
excerpt:
Aston Martin recorded a loss of £28.5 million GBP after tax during the year ending December 31st, 2025 documents show.

The F1 team is owned and operated by AMR GP Limited, based at Silverstone, and submitted its yearly required accounts to Companies House, showing its turnover, gross profit, and loses.

AMR GP Limited recorded a turnover of £344.234 million GBP in the 2025 year, a rise from £280.683 million in the same period to December 31st, 2024. The turnover is made up of prize money from Formula 1 for the team's performance in the constructors' championship and its own commercial revenue from sponsorship.

AMR GP Limited then posted cost of sales of £199.122 million GBP in 2025, leaving a gross profit of £145.112 million GBP. This was a climb from a cost of sales of £181.090 million in 2024 to a gross profit of £99.593 million.

This represents a near £46 million GBP rise in gross profit year-on-year.

However, an operating loss of £20.537 million was recorded, leading to a loss before tax in the 2025 year of £51.653 million which was reduced to £41.072 million once tax was factored out.

Once "other comprehensive income" was added, it meant AMR GP Limited recorded a total loss of £28.452 million GBP.

In the same period in 2024, the loss before tax was £39.618 million, not including tax, which pushed the final bottom line figure to £45.793 million.

It means year-on-year, AMR GP Limited reduced its losses by £17.341 million GBP.

The results come after the team has recently completed building its brand-new campus at Silverstone, with a state-of-the-art factory, including an all-new wind-tunnel, being used by Adrian Newey and his design team after Newey joined from Red Bull.

The team, which grew its headcount by 151 people to 996 in 2025, up from 845 in 2024, also counted various new sponsors which will be reflected in the 2026 accounts, including Cognition, Cohere, Brietling, CoinPayments, and Eight Sleep.

The submission is part of a mandatory requirement from all F1 teams based in the UK, with Mercedes previously reporting theirs in June. F1 itself also reported its returns earlier this month.

RacingNews365 examined Williams' accounts on Tuesday, with McLaren, Red Bull, and Alpine all expected later on Wednesday, September 30th.

title: Lewis Hamilton claims radical F1 decision 'makes no sense'
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton believes the decision to host a Sprint event at next year's Monaco Grand Prix "makes no sense."

For the first time, the event in the Principality will host F1's shorter race format in 2027, one of a record number of 10 Sprints dotted across the season, including both the season-opener and season-finale in Bahrain and Abu Dhabi, respectively.

F1's rationale behind the decision is that given qualifying in Monaco is often deemed one of the best days of the season, there will be two qualifying sessions to look forward to with the Sprint format - with Sprint Qualifying taking place after just one hour of practice.

It is hoped that this could create different grids for both events, but Hamilton, who has won the Monaco GP three times, believes adding a Sprint is not the answer to the surgery Monaco needs to address its chronic lack of overtaking.

"It makes no sense to me, but I'm not making the decisions, obviously," Hamilton told media, including RacingNews365.

"So, on the positive, maybe we get another qualifying session, which is quite cool. But I've always said Monaco needs something different.

"It can't be... I don't think it should be the same race formula that it is everywhere else. It needs to be something different.

"We've already included the sprint races, which I think have really brought something new to the sport.

"But I think we've got to come up with something new for somewhere like that, because it's a beautiful place, such a beautiful country, an incredible circuit to drive."

The article continues below.

'As dull as it gets'

In response to the 2024 race where the entire field was able to change tyres after a first-lap red flag, for 2025, a mandatory two-stop strategy was implemented.

This led to drivers deliberately blocking rivals to allow their team-mates to complete the two stops and not lose position.

For 2026, the race returned to a normal format, and although there was some excitement with the red flag for the track breaking up, it was still a race with a dearth of overtaking.

Hamilton believes that the Sprint is "not the answer."

"The race is as dull as it gets," he said.

"So I don't know, but the Sprint race is not the answer, I would say."

title: Liam Lawson handed F1 seat backing as 'unchanged' Racing Bulls line-up predicted
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has not yet had any assurances about his spot on the F1 grid for the 2027 season.

Former IndyCar driver James Hinchcliffe has backed Liam Lawson to keep his seat at Racing Bulls for the 2027 season.

The Red Bull sister squad has not yet confirmed its line-up for next year as it mulls over its options.

While Arvid Lindblad is expected to retain his seat following an impressive rookie campaign, Liam Lawson's position is less clear despite a strong season thus far.

Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov is waiting in the wings for a promotion to F1 as he fights for the F2 championship in his rookie season.

But having scored over 55 per cent of Racing Bulls' points this year, Hinchcliffe believes Lawson has done enough to keep his drive.

"He's done plenty to justify being back at that team," Hinchcliffe told the F1 Nation podcast.

"I imagine that lineup's unchanged next year. It just stings right now."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Liam Lawson

New Zealander

30

Lawson radio frustration a 'natural' reaction

Lawson retired from last weekend's race in Baku after a coming together with teammate Arvid Lindblad during a safety car restart.

The New Zealander conveyed a frustrated message over the team radio about being taken out by the other Racing Bulls driver, but Hinchcliffe insisted it was a raw reaction to the high-pressure situation.

"That's a natural reaction in the moment," he said.

"I mean, you'll get over that stuff. It was nothing Lawson did wrong.

"There's nothing in that moment that the team can use against him in the case of whether or not he should be back there next year."

Racing driver and Hinchcliffe's podcast co-host Alex Brundle insisted Lawson can be proud of his season, which included a brief step up to the Red Bull team.

"Hopping up to the main team, delivering the performances, hopping back down again, being on the pace, I completely agree," he said.

"At least you can go back to the garage with your head held high and go, 'Well, I was taken out of the race today. What is it you want to do me about it? I was ahead of that guy because that's how I ended up backwards in the runoff area'."

title: Colton Herta refuses to let F1 dream die despite major F2 struggles
excerpt:
Colton Herta says his focus is still "getting to F1", despite a disappointing first season in FIA Formula 2.

Herta left IndyCar to follow his dream of making it to grand prix racing in 2026, and joined the Hitech F2 team to build up experience on Pirelli tyres and within a European style of racing, but it has been a poor season.

Herta has just 26 points to his name thus far, with a best of fifth in the reversed-grid Barcelona Sprint race, where he was third on the grid, and has made clear that he does not intend to return in 2027.

He has supplemented his running in FIA F2 with FP1 practice outings for Cadillac in F1, doing so in Barcelona, Hungary, Italy, and at one other race to be announced, although it will likely be Austin.

Herta still does not have enough points to qualify for the required FIA superlicence, with the American currently on 38 points, through his IndyCar performances between 2023-2025, plus points earned during his FP1 outings.

He will lose one point for his 10th place finish in 2023 in IndyCar at the end of this season as the three-year rolling cycle moves to 2024, with Herta facing a 'make or bust' situation at the end of 2027.

There, the 30 points he earned for finishing as runner-up in 2024, making up the bulk of his tally, will fall away, meaning he must race in an appropriately rewarded championship - but he has not given up hope of reaching F1.

"It all depends on what next year looks like. My focus is still on getting to F1, and I still think I have a chance of that in these next two years," Herta told Autosport.

"But I don't know exactly; I have to sit back and see what the plan is for Cadillac for me.

"And once I know that, then I can make more decisions on maybe if I'm in Formula 1, if I'm not. What does that look like in terms of, is it a reserve role? Is it still a test role? If that's the case, what other series can I race in during that to stay busy?

"So, there's a lot of just, like, nothing to say at the moment, unfortunately, until I have more solidified plans for next year – then I can build everything out around that.

"I don't have anything for next year at the moment, but we're discussing getting through that as far as what the opportunities are for me within the team."

The article continues below.

Herta to F1?

Clarifying his recent remarks, Herta spoke of the "zero progression" he was showing in FIA F2.

"I said 'I don't have an interest,'" Herta said.

"This year, I think if there was clear progression and whatnot, it would be more interesting to return, but there's zero progression.

“I've been doing a lot more with the F1 team now as far as sim stuff. I just did a TPC [Testing of Previous Cars] day which was very strong. On the F1 sim and the TPC stuff, the pace has been really strong, but for whatever reason, it's just not translating to F2."

title: Fernando Alonso teases 'moment of truth' after slide to F1 'anonymity'
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso says he is "at peace" with his current 'anonymity' in F1 and teased that Aston Martin is "preparing ourselves for a moment of truth."

The two-time F1 champion announced on Tuesday that he would be returning for the 2027 season, ending months of speculation over whether he would call time on a grand prix career which has yielded two drivers' titles, in 2005 and 2006, 32 wins, and 106 podiums.

By the end of the 2027 season, in which he will become the first 46-year-old to compete in F1 since Maurice Trintignant at the 1964 French GP, Alonso is on course to rack up 472 grand prix starts - or a remarkable 39.46% of all 1,196 grands prix up to, and including, the 2027 Abu Dhabi GP.

Given the uncompetitive nature of his Aston Martin-Honda package in 2026, Alonso has only been able to score points twice, in Monaco and in the Netherlands, as the team looks to work through its issues and return to competitiveness.

As the team has slid to the rear of the field, it therefore does not earn as much TV time on the world broadcast feed, as opposed to battles for the lead or podium places, something Alonso says he has made "peace with."

"At the moment, I feel it was not the time because I'm better than that guy. I'm better than that other guy. I will think like that. And I cannot stop racing if I still think like that," he told BBC Sport.

"You only prove to people when you are on the podium, or you are on TV. That's where eyes are open, and people remember suddenly that you're still on the grid.

"So now I'm at peace with this period of time that I'm anonymous, and no one knows that we're still there and we're still fast.

"We are preparing ourselves for the moment of truth, and that will be a surprise for everybody again."

The article continues below.

Alonso still feels better than rivals

Explaining how he compared himself to rivals, Alonso described how he still felt he had the competitive edge over some drivers - and when he lost that, is when he would decide to "watch the race from my living room."

"When I jump in the car, in free practice, I will see some people braking late in a corner, locking up the front tyres here or there, making mistakes there," he continued.

"I feel that I'm OK. Or, I'm faster than them.

"So when I get changed, and I go back home, even if I'm P18, in a way I feel some satisfaction and pride inside, even if it should not be the case because we are not competitive.

"How will I be in the living room, watching TV, thinking that I can do better? That will be my feeling now. When that changes, if I see that I lost abilities, I lost speed, I lost reflexes, I lost something, then I will be happy to watch the race from my living room.

title: Williams halve financial loss after best F1 season for decade
excerpt:
Williams halved its financial loss in the 2025 financial year, after enjoying its best season on-track in a decade.

Official legal documents submitted to Companies House show the team posted a loss, before tax of £19.644 million GBP, which, when tax was applied, gave a loss of £25.115 million for the year ending December 31st.

This was a fall from a pre-tax loss of £42.251 million in the 2024 period, which was a total loss of £49.896 million.

It means Williams posted a loss 50.32% less in 2025 than in 2024, with a chunk of the loss being absorbed by greater prize money from Formula One Management for its 2025 showing, in which it finished fifth in the standings as opposed to ninth in 2024.

The team enjoyed its most successful campaign on-track in 2025 since 2016, with new signing Carlos Sainz scoring two grand prix podiums in Azerbaijan and Qatar, in addition to third in the United States GP Sprint - Williams' first podium in a Sprint.

Williams derives its income from championship prize money and commercial sponsorship.

This is evidenced by its turnover in 2025, which was £243.976 million GBP, a climb from £179.776 million GBP in 2024, a rise of £64.2 million GBP.

After cost of sales were factored in, it left Williams with a gross profit of £93.809 million GBP in 2025, a rise from £72.576 million GBP in 2024 - although it did register sales around £43 million greater in 2025 than 2024.

After assets were calculated, it means the team had £98.595 million in cash reserves in 2025, compared to £130.077 million in 2024.

In the documents, director Matthew Savage explained that the overall 2025 loss was "in line with expectations."

"Whilst the group remains in a loss position, this is in line with expectations and the group's strategy to continue investing in all areas of the business to drive both on-track and commercial performance in pursuit of success in the medium and long-term," he said.

Savage also pointed to the array of new sponsors as a "vote of confidence" in the team.

"In a further vote of confidence in the team's ambition and momentum, the team added several major new commercial partners into the 2026 season: Barclays, Anthropic, BNY, Wilkinson Sword, Estrella Galicia, Nuveen, New Era and Giraud-Perregaux," continued the statement.

Williams has also invested in its driver academy to help create the "champions of the future", and indicated that the Williams group will "continue to expand its industry-leading STEM schools outreach programme which brought more than 12,000 8-to-16 year-olds to our Grove HQ free of charge to experience STEM careers through the lens of motorsport."

The team also grew its headcount in 2025 to 1,151 people, a climb of around 200.

Other UK-based F1 teams are required to share their financial records for the year by Wednesday, September 30th, including Alpine, McLaren, and Red Bull.

Red Bull's accounts should show the figures paid to Christian Horner and Helmut Marko on their departures.

Mercedes filed its accounts in June, with F1 doing so last week, and is available here.

title: Fred Vasseur defended as Ferrari job scrutiny grows
excerpt:
Recent reports have suggested that Fred Vasseur's position at the head of Ferrari may no longer be assured.

Former IndyCar driver James Hinchcliffe has jumped to the defence of Fred Vasseur as speculation over his F1 future grows.

In recent weeks, Vasseur's position at Ferrari has been questioned by Italian media outlets, with former Red Bull boss Christian Horner publicly voicing his interest in taking on the team principal role at the squad.

Ferrari entered the 2026 campaign hoping to field a competitive car and challenge for the F1 title, having not achieved championship success since the 2008 season.

However, bar a couple of race wins, it has not been able to match the pace of Mercedes, who look set for a convincing double-championship triumph.

With Vasseur's future within the team now seemingly less assured, Hinchcliffe stated it is part of the challenge that comes with leading the team.

"It's the double-edged sword of being Ferrari," Hinchcliffe told the F1 Nation podcast.

"You are the oldest, most tenured, most beloved, most revered team on the grid.

"I do think that they get undue criticism sometimes and maybe undue praise at the same time."

[Article continues below]

Vasseur good at 'addressing the noise' around Ferrari

Shortly after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend, Ferrari issued a statement in which it outlined that it had "full confidence" in Vasseur.

While Ferrari has not been able to make an impact in the championship fight since Vasseur took over in 2023, Hinchcliffe insisted the Frenchman has sparked positive change.

He noted that Vasseur has been able to instil a working culture that is not impacted by the constant pressure to deliver that comes with Ferrari's F1 status.

"What Fred has been very good at is addressing the noise, but being able to block it out and protect the people internally.

"That's been one of the bigger issues in years past and under different leaders, it seeps into the team.

"Fred has done a really good job at being the point guard there, being the gatekeeper to all of that noise, good and bad, and protecting the team, letting them get on with the job."

title: George Russell assigns 'most dominant' verdict as F1 title hopes reignited
excerpt:
George Russel picked up his first career Grand Slam last weekend in Baku as he scored his third win of the season.

George Russell has stated his display at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix marked the “most dominant” weekend he has enjoyed in his career.

Russell took pole position by a mammoth eight-tenths of a second, the biggest margin seen in F1 since the 2023 Canadian Grand Prix.

He went on to lead every lap of the race to win it with the fastest lap in hand, despite some late pressure from Max Verstappen, who was seeking his first trip to the top step of the podium this year.

However, Russell went on to narrow the gap in the standings to Kimi Antonelli to 66 points, with the latter crossing the line in fifth in a recovery drive after crashing in qualifying.

Having struggled for form of late, Russell stated his outing in Baku marked his strongest showing yet in F1.

“It’s my first Grand Slam in Formula 1 and, for sure, the most dominant weekend I’ve had in my career,” Russell told media including RacingNews365.

“So that has come at a really great moment.”

Driver

George Russell

British

63

'Easy to lose faith in the season'

Prior to the Baku weekend, Russell was sitting 81 points down on Antonelli in the standings, with his championship hopes rapidly fading.

However, with a boost in confidence now under his belt, Russell will be hoping to continue to eat into the deficit in the coming rounds.

“Also to achieve it on a circuit that requires so much commitment and confidence, I’m really proud of,” he said.

“I think it would have been very easy for me to lose the faith this season.

“Not necessarily about winning the championship, but in terms of my ability, and that never happened.”

title: Mercedes overtake Ferrari to become most successful F1 manufacturer of all-time
excerpt:
Mercedes has become the most successful F1 engine manufacturer in terms of race wins, ending Ferrari's 22-year reign.

George Russell's victory in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix was the 252nd for a Mercedes engine in grand prix racing, passing the 251 benchmark Ferrari had set with Charles Leclerc's victory at the British GP earlier this year.

The first driver to win with a Mercedes engine was Juan Manuel Fangio at the 1954 French GP, on Mercedes-Benz's grand prix debut, with the team going onto claim nine grand prix wins before withdrawing after 1955 in the wake of the Le Mans disaster.

Mercedes power would not return to F1 until the late 1990s, with David Coulthard claiming Mercedes' 10th victory at the 1997 Australian GP in the back of a McLaren. By this time, Ferrari had 108 wins, although it had experienced a lean period in the early and mid-1990s.

By the time of the 2004 British Grand Prix, the team moved ahead of Ford Cosworth with its 180th victory, courtesy of Michael Schumacher.

Over the course of the last 22 seasons, Ferrari extended its record to 251, with Mercedes on 99 by the time of the adoption of the turbo hybrid era in 2014.

This means since the start of 2014, Mercedes power has won 153 grands prix, compared to 29 for Ferrari.

The wins of Mercedes power is split between the Mercedes works team, McLaren, Brawn GP, and Racing Point, whilst Ferrari has won 250 of the 251 grands prix won by Ferrari engines.

Sebastian Vettel remains the only driver to ever win a grand prix using a Ferrari engine not in a Ferrari chassis, doing so when he won the 2008 Italian Grand Prix for Toro Rosso, using a customer Ferrari engine.

title: McLaren point to 'high priority' focus after Lando Norris concern
excerpt:
Lando Norris endured a highly challenging Azerbaijan Grand Prix last weekend, which ended in a retirement.

McLaren has vowed to look into an issue that plagued Lando Norris during the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, labelling it as a "high priority".

The reigning champion endured a difficult outing last weekend as he appeared to lack pace in the opening half of the race.

After the event, McLaren team principal Andrea Stella indicated that he was suffering from a "fuel injection" concern that the squad will now analyse.

The Italian asserted that it was a "high priority" area it will work on ahead of the next race weekend, which will be held in Malaysia.

"On Lando's side, we were struggling a little bit with power unit deployment, and also Lando was having some inconsistencies in his driving," Stella told media including RacingNews365.

"When he was overtaken by [Lewis] Hamilton, he had a lock-up, and he had a few mistakes that meant that cars behind were within range.

"And when they are within range, then we struggle to defend, which goes back to the point on top speed."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Lando Norris

British

1

McLaren take blame for underwhelming Lando Norris outing

Norris' race ended on lap 36 when he was involved in a multi-car collision during a safety car restart.

While his race lacked promise in the build-up to his early exit, Stella asserted it was the fault of the team, rather than the driver.

"I would say that for Lando, this was one of the most difficult events in general that he has experienced in 2026.

"It's something that we need to take away, looking at whatever can be improved.

"But I would say most of the opportunities lie on the team side, and on the car side, because we need to be able to offer our drivers a car that is more raceable and just more consistent in terms of predictability.”

At the front of the grid, McLaren and Ferrari will keep their line-ups intact, while Max Verstappen will remain at Red Bull following months of speculation.

The four-time champion has penned a new deal to remain with the team until the end of 2030, before Isack Hadjar was also announced on a new deal.

Mercedes has not yet announced its line-up for 2027, but it is widely expected that Kimi Antonelli and George Russell will remain in place.

At Williams, Alexander Albon signed a one-year extension earlier this year, with Carlos Sainz's announcement following a day later on a new multi-year deal.

Franco Colapinto has been signed to continue at Alpine, while Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas are both confirmed at Cadillac as the American outfit builds towards its second season on the grid.

Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll will once again form Aston Martin's line-up, as will Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto at Audi.

It means, as of September 29th, there are just six seats remaining on the grid - at Mercedes, Racing Bulls, and Haas.

title: Has Fernando Alonso made the right decision to remain with Aston Martin?
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has confirmed he will remain at Aston Martin for the 2027 season, ending speculation over his long-term future in Formula 1.

The two-time world champion has endured a difficult year with the Silverstone-based outfit, sitting 19th in the drivers' standings with just three points after 15 rounds.

Alonso retired from the Azerbaijan Grand Prix last time out, citing an unexplained loss of around 1.5 seconds per lap on the straights, despite Honda telemetry showing no obvious faults.

The Spaniard has also dealt with severe cockpit vibrations from the Honda power unit throughout the campaign, which caused numbness in his hands and feet and sparked early-season concerns over potential nerve damage.

Technical boss Adrian Newey has already identified a development overhaul for next year, with refined power unit ratios planned to improve integration between chassis and engine.

Alonso has previously indicated that his decision on racing beyond 2026 hinges more on the broader direction of the sport's regulations than on Aston Martin's current competitiveness.

But has he made the right call? Have your say below!

title: Fernando Alonso explains decision to delay F1 retirement
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has explained the key factors behind his decision to delay his F1 retirement and extend his stay in grand prix racing.

The two-time world champion has been weighing up whether to return for a 24th season in 2027 or to call time on an F1 career which has yielded the 2005 and 2006 drivers' titles, 32 grand prix victories, and 106 podiums so far.

Ultimately, the Spanish veteran of 440 F1 starts, has decided to stay on with Aston Martin as it looks to climb up the pecking order following a poor start to the new 2026 rules with engine partner Honda.

Alonso has scored just three points thus far in 2026 from a 10th in Monaco and a ninth in the Netherlands, with both the Aston Martin chassis and Honda engine being below expectations - but Alonso has decided to give the partnership another year.

“I'm very happy to sign a new contract with the Aston Martin,” Alonso said.

“I took my time to make this decision, but racing is my life, my passion, and I know I still have the speed and determination to compete at the highest level. I’m committed for the long term with this team and to helping us succeed.

“I truly believe in what we are building: we have strong leadership, incredible people, partners and facilities.

“I look forward to making more memories on the race track in front of the passionate fans.

“Their energy creates an atmosphere that inspires me and is what makes our sport special.”

Stroll heads into seventh season with Aston Martin

Aston Martin has also confirmed that Stroll will continue in the seat alongside Alonso, marking their fifth year together as team-mates.

Delivering his reaction to the extension, Stroll stated: “I’m very happy to continue with Aston Martin for the long term.

“I’ve been on this journey since the beginning and I believe we have the resources and the people to become a winning team.

“There is so much hard work going on at Silverstone with real progress being made, and the determination I see in every department is a huge motivation for me.

“I know we are heading in the right direction, and my commitment is stronger than ever to help us achieve our goals.”

title: Fernando Alonso announces decision over possible F1 retirement
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has announced he will return to Formula 1 for the 2027 season, and delay his retirement from grand prix racing for at least another year as Aston Martin confirmed its driver line-up.

The Spanish driver, the 2005 and 2006 world champion, has been weighing up whether to return for a 24th season in 2027 amid the ongoing struggles of the Aston Martin-Honda package.

He will be joined for a fifth season by Lance Stroll, who also confirmed his extension to what the team have called "long-term contracts."

Alonso, the most experienced driver in F1 history, with a total of 440 starts, joined Aston Martin in 2023 after leaving Alpine and enjoyed immediate success, with eight podiums in the first season.

However, the team slipped down the pecking order over the following seasons and hit rock bottom at the start of 2026, with the Adrian Newey-designed machine unreliable and suffering from severe vibrations from its Honda power unit.

Alonso picked up a point in the Monaco GP before a B-spec car was introduced in Hungary, with a new Honda engine in the Netherlands, where Alonso took ninth for two points.

The former go-karter from Oviedo has made clear his dissatisfaction with the 2026 F1 rules, describing fast corners as "charging stations" for the batteries and saying that the challenge of driving cars has been reduced.

However, Alonso has now decided to return for 2027 and will extend his career into a 24th season, in which he will pass 450 grands prix entered and started.

title: Bahrain GP in Malaysia: Every time F1 raced using a different country's name
excerpt:
This weekend we will have a grand prix held in a different country from the name it suggests - but what other instances of this have we seen during F1's history?

F1 arrives at Sepang this week for a race that will not go anywhere near the country in its name.

The Bahrain Grand Prix has been relocated to Malaysia, with the Sepang International Circuit hosting the Gulf Air-backed event after Bahrain International Circuit was ruled out following a postponement of the original April date and subsequent security concerns across the Middle East.

Bahrain is understood to be helping fund the move, while retaining its national airline's title sponsorship.

It is far from the first time a grand prix name and its venue have gone their separate ways.

The 1982 Swiss Grand Prix

Switzerland has not hosted a round of the world championship on home soil since 1954, after the country banned circuit motor racing in the wake of the 1955 Le Mans disaster.

That did not stop the calendar from carrying a Swiss Grand Prix in 1982, run instead at Dijon-Prenois in France.

Keke Rosberg won from eighth on the grid for Williams, with Alain Prost's Renault second and Niki Lauda completing the podium for McLaren.

The 1981-2006 San Marino Grand Prix

For 26 years, the San Marino Grand Prix was one of the fixtures of the European season, and yet the race never came close to the tiny republic whose name it carried.

FIA rules allowed each nation only one national grand prix, and Italy's was already spoken for by Monza. San Marino, in any case, had neither the terrain nor an FIA-standard circuit to host F1.

The solution was to borrow the neighbouring enclave's identity for a race staged at Imola, just across the Italian border, which became a fixture of the calendar until its final running in 2006.

The 1997-1998 Luxembourg Grand Prix

The same logic produced the Luxembourg Grand Prix, held in 1997 and 1998 not in Luxembourg but at the Nurburgring in Germany.

Hockenheim already held the contractual rights to the German Grand Prix, and regulations barred two races in the same country from sharing a national title, so organisers reached for Luxembourg instead, whose border sits roughly 80 kilometres from the Nürburgring.

Jacques Villeneuve won the 1997 edition for Williams ahead of Jean Alesi's Benetton, while Mika Hakkinen took victory in 1998 from Michael Schumacher's Ferrari.

The many locations of the European Grand Prix

The European Grand Prix name went further still, appearing across six circuits in three different countries: Brands Hatch and Donington Park in Britain, the Nürburgring in Germany, Jerez and the Valencia street circuit in Spain, and Baku in Azerbaijan.

The title was historically used as a way of squeezing a second race into a country's season without breaching the one-grand-prix-per-nation rule, and it also served as the promotional label for Baku's inaugural 2016 race before the event was renamed the Azerbaijan Grand Prix the following year.
